topic: Diagnosing sign and conjugate errors with complex numbers
subtitle: Finding and fixing sign and conjugate errors

traps.desc: treated i squared as +1, so the last term subtracted instead of adding
applied the minus sign to the real part only
applied the minus sign to the real part only, leaving plus 2i minus 6i

problems.desc: Rubric for the diagnosis. A full-credit answer says the minus sign in front of the second number must be distributed to BOTH of its parts, so the imaginary term becomes plus six i and not minus six i, and that the printed work changed only the real part. Accept any wording that identifies the undistributed minus sign. No credit for writing the correct value again with no statement of what went wrong.

traps.desc: multiplied out the conjugate correctly but computed the new denominator as 9 minus 4 instead of 9 plus 4

problems.desc: Rubric for the diagnosis. A full-credit answer says the denominator of a conjugate product is a SUM of squares, because the minus times minus on the i terms combines with i squared equal to negative one, so the value is nine plus four and not nine minus four. Accept wording that identifies the denominator as the wrong line and gives the correct value thirteen. No credit for correcting the arithmetic without naming which line was wrong.

traps.desc: squared each term on its own and dropped the middle term

problems.desc: Rubric for the diagnosis. A full-credit answer says that squaring a binomial is a product of two binomials, so the middle term of twice five times two i must appear, and the printed work squared each term separately. Accept an answer that names the missing middle term or writes out the four products. No credit for a corrected value with no statement of the missing term.

traps.desc: kept the sign of the second number instead of reversing both of its parts
multiplied the denominator by the conjugate but left the numerator alone

problems.slot: the first wrong line and the rule
problems.desc: Rubric for the diagnosis. A full-credit answer points at the second line of the printed work, where the conjugate was multiplied into the denominator only, and states the rule: multiplying by a conjugate over itself is multiplying by one, so BOTH the numerator and the denominator must gain the factor or the value of the fraction changes. Accept an answer that checks the result by multiplying it back by the original denominator. No credit for naming a later line, since every later line follows correctly from that one.
